chapter_title: Security Best Practices for Smart Contracts

screens.title: Security Best Practices for Smart Contracts
screens.subtitle: Defend immutable on-chain code with patterns, libraries, and verification

narration.text: Smart contracts are immutable programs that control value on-chain, so a single bug can cause permanent loss. In this lesson you will learn the most common vulnerabilities—reentrancy, integer overflow and underflow, and front-running—and how to prevent them with secure coding patterns and battle-tested libraries. You will also learn when to apply access control with Ownable or a role-based AccessControl design, how OpenZeppelin Contracts reduce risk, and why external audits and formal verification matter for critical systems. We’ll connect practical controls, code examples, and hands-on tests so you can see both the attack and the fix. For example, you will see a vulnerable withdrawal function that updates balances after sending funds, and then compare it to a secure variant that uses checks, effects, and interactions plus a reentrancy guard. Throughout, I’ll point out common misconceptions, like thinking gas limits always prevent reentrancy or believing timestamps are safe for randomness. By the end you’ll be able to apply these defensive patterns and decide when to invest in auditing or formal proofs. Ask yourself: which contract in your project handles real funds and needs extra review?

keyIdea.title: Security is a design-first concern
keyIdea.text: Immutable contracts require preventive design: use simple logic, battle-tested libraries, access controls, and formal review to reduce risk.

screens.title: Learning Objectives (Part 1)
screens.subtitle: Skills you will gain and why they matter

narration.text: Over the next screens you will build a practical mental model of common smart contract vulnerabilities and the controls that stop them. First, you will learn to identify reentrancy attacks and why ordering of checks, effects, and interactions prevents them. Second, you will understand integer overflow and underflow risks, why modern Solidity reverts on these arithmetic errors, and how older projects used SafeMath to avoid wrapping behavior. Third, you will apply OpenZeppelin’s contracts to add proven building blocks instead of inventing your own. Finally, you will implement basic access control with Ownable and prepare to use role-based AccessControl when multiple administrators are needed. Each objective ties to a practical lab step so you can see an exploit and then fix it. Keep in mind: recognizing a vulnerability is as important as fixing it—incorrect fixes can make problems worse. As you learn, think about which contracts in your codebase manage value, and which need immediate protection or an audit.

keyIdea.title: From detection to defense
keyIdea.text: Learning to spot vulnerabilities and apply community-vetted controls reduces the chance of costly exploits.

narration.text: These next objectives focus on protective judgement and practical safeguards. You will learn to design commit-reveal schemes and other transaction-order-resistant patterns to reduce front-running risk, and recognize when contract logic should avoid exposing sensitive state in a mempool. You will also apply secure randomness practices: why block attributes are manipulable and how to rely on oracle-based randomness for production systems. Finally, you will understand the role of auditing and formal verification—when to choose one or both—and how reducing contract complexity makes verification more feasible. Each objective includes a concrete example: a simple commit-reveal auction to prevent frontrunning, an explanation of using Chainlink VRF for randomness rather than timestamps, and criteria to decide whether a high-value contract needs a formal proof. These skills help you balance cost and risk when protecting funds on-chain.

narration.text: Smart contracts run autonomously once deployed and cannot be changed without an upgrade path or redeployment. That immutability means bugs are not just annoying — they can permanently lock or lose funds. A practical example: a flawed withdrawal function that updates state after sending funds can allow an attacker to repeatedly extract value. The lesson here is that security begins in design: minimize mutable state with straightforward logic and rely on community-reviewed libraries where possible. A common misconception is that tests alone are sufficient. Tests are essential, but they cannot cover every execution path, especially when adversaries intentionally try to exploit edge cases. This is why layered defenses are necessary: private tests, fuzzing, static analysis, external audits, and, when appropriate, formal verification. Another useful practice is to limit the blast radius: split responsibilities across minimal contracts, keep administrative privileges tightly scoped with access control patterns, and add failsafe switches such as a pausable mechanism or multisignature administrative wallets. Thinking defensively at design time reduces the chances you'll need expensive remediation later. Reflect on the contracts you maintain: which state changes carry financial risk and deserve extra scrutiny?

keyIdea.title: Design first, secure always
keyIdea.text: Immutable deployment requires defensive design: simplicity, vetted libraries, and layered review protect value.

content.html:
Core Concept

Why smart contract security matters

Immutability and value make smart contract bugs costly. Design choices reduce risk.

Quick Example
A withdrawal function that sends funds before updating the balance can be reentered by a malicious contract and drained.
Defensive checklist
  • Prefer simple logic and small contracts that are easier to audit and reason about.
  • Use require and revert to validate inputs early and avoid invalid state transitions.
  • Apply access control for critical functions and use multi-sig for high-risk admin actions.
  • Plan failsafes: pausable contracts and emergency stops reduce blast radius during incidents.
Common mistake: assuming test coverage finds malicious exploit paths. Tests help but don’t guarantee security.
Concrete scenario
Imagine a token migration function that transfers user balances. If migration can be called twice due to missing checks, users lose funds. Designing with clear ownership, require checks, and one-time flags prevents repeated executions.
Pro tip: map high-risk functions and prioritize audits for the smallest contract that holds the most value.
Key Takeaway

Security is primarily a design concern: reduce complexity, attach guards, and treat audits as part of your delivery process.

screens.title: Reentrancy and the Checks-Effects-Interactions pattern
screens.subtitle: How ordering prevents repeated external calls

narration.text: Reentrancy occurs when your contract makes an external call and the external contract calls back into your contract before your function has finished. The canonical attack withdraws funds in a loop because the attacker is able to call into the contract repeatedly while the victim’s state still reflects the withdrawable balance. The mitigation centers on ordering: check preconditions, apply effects to state, then make interactions. This ensures the contract’s visible state already reflects the withdrawal before any external call can observe or reenter. Concrete example: if you require that the caller has a sufficient balance, then decrement the balance immediately, and only afterwards call the external address to transfer ETH, a reentrant fallback cannot withdraw more than allowed. A common misconception is that using transfer or send removes all risk; these methods limit gas forwarded but are not a substitute for correct state ordering. Another defense is to use a reentrancy guard that prevents functions from being reentered in the same call stack. Closing takeaway: ordering and a guard together make reentrancy attacks far harder. Ask yourself: where in your contract could an external call observe stale state?

keyIdea.title: Order matters
keyIdea.text: Checks, then Effects, then Interactions ensures state is updated before any external call can exploit it.

content.html:
Process Flow

Reentrancy & Checks-Effects-Interactions

Learn the defensive sequence and how it stops reentrant callers.

Checks → Effects → Interactions
  1. Checks: Validate requirements and inputs, e.g., balance sufficiency.
  2. Effects: Update state variables so the contract reflects the new reality.
  3. Interactions: Make external calls or transfers only after state is safe.
Misconception: relying on gas-limited transfers alone is fragile; explicit ordering is a stronger defense.
Annotated example
Imagine withdraw flow: require(balance >= amount); balance -= amount; (bool success, ) = msg.sender.call{value: amount}(''); require(success); This order prevents reentry from seeing the old balance.
Common mistake: updating balances after the external call.
Pro tip: combine ordering with a nonReentrant guard for extra safety.
Key Takeaway

Always update state before external calls and consider a reentrancy guard to block recursive entry.

screens.title: Vulnerable vs Secure: Withdraw function walkthrough
screens.subtitle: Compare VulnerableBank and SecureBank implementations

narration.text: We’ll walk through two concrete contracts so you can see the exploit and the fix. The vulnerable contract performs an external call to the caller before decrementing their balance. That ordering allows a malicious fallback to reenter and call withdraw again while the original balance still exists. The secure contract uses OpenZeppelin’s ReentrancyGuard and/or the checks-effects-interactions ordering. It updates the balance before making the external call and marks the withdraw function as nonReentrant. Concrete example in practice: deploy the vulnerable contract, deposit funds, then use a malicious contract that triggers its fallback to call withdraw repeatedly; the attacker drains the balance. In contrast, the secure contract prevents reentrant execution or ensures the balance was already reduced before any external call. A common misconception is to assume only highly skilled attackers exploit these issues; in reality, automated bots scan for these patterns. The closing question is: after you review withdraws in your codebase, where will you add explicit state updates and reentrancy protection? In practical terms, compare vulnerablebank and securebank implementations. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: See the exploit to learn the fix

content.html:
Code Walkthrough

VulnerableBank vs SecureBank

Compare the exact withdraw flow and see how OpenZeppelin utilities fit in.

VulnerableBank.sol (excerpt)
// SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
pragma solidity ^0.8.20;

contract VulnerableBank {
  mapping(address => uint256) public balances;

  function deposit() public payable {
    balances[msg.sender] += msg.value;
  }

  // VULNERABLE WITHDRAW FUNCTION
  function withdraw(uint256 _amount) public {
    require(balances[msg.sender] >= _amount, "Insufficient balance");

    // External call before state update - REENTRANCY VULNERABILITY
    (bool success, ) = msg.sender.call{value: _amount}("");
    require(success, "Transfer failed");

    balances[msg.sender] -= _amount; // State updated AFTER external call
  }
}
Vulnerable because state is decremented after the external call, enabling reentry.
SecureBank.sol (excerpt)
// SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
pragma solidity ^0.8.20;

import "@openzeppelin/contracts/access/Ownable.sol";
import "@openzeppelin/contracts/utils/ReentrancyGuard.sol";

contract SecureBank is Ownable, ReentrancyGuard {
  mapping(address => uint256) public balances;

  constructor() Ownable(msg.sender) {}

  function deposit() public payable {
    balances[msg.sender] += msg.value;
  }

  // SECURE WITHDRAW FUNCTION
  function withdraw(uint256 _amount) public nonReentrant {
    require(balances[msg.sender] >= _amount, "Insufficient balance");

    balances[msg.sender] -= _amount; // State updated BEFORE external call

    (bool success, ) = msg.sender.call{value: _amount}("");
    require(success, "Transfer failed");
  }
}
Secure because state is updated first and the nonReentrant modifier blocks recursive entry.
Example scenario
Deploy the vulnerable contract, deposit some ETH, then run a malicious contract that calls withdraw inside its fallback. The attacker can loop until drained. Test the secure contract the same way to see the guard and ordering block the drain.

screens.title: Integer Overflow and Underflow
screens.subtitle: Why arithmetic wrapping used to be dangerous and how Solidity changed

narration.text: Integer overflow and underflow happen when arithmetic results fall outside the range for a numeric type. For unsigned integers, underflow means subtracting more than the value and wrapping around to a very large number. Historically, this wrapping was a common source of exploits: arithmetic could silently produce values that change critical logic, for instance granting an attacker an enormous token balance. Since Solidity 0.8.0 arithmetic operations revert on overflow and underflow by default, which prevents silent wrapping and makes contracts safer. If you must interact with older code or use libraries compiled for older compilers, use SafeMath or equivalent checks to avoid silent wrap behavior. A common misconception is that changing the compiler version automatically makes all older patterns safe; you must audit older contracts and their published bytecode. Concrete example: an 8-bit unsigned value at 255 adding one wraps to zero on older runtimes; today that addition would revert instead. Takeaway: prefer Solidity 0.8+ and explicit checks when porting legacy code, and include numeric bounds checks in critical financial arithmetic. Integer Overflow and Underflow means use solidity 0.8+ for built-in overflow checks; audit or patch older code that relied on safemath semantics.. In practical terms, why arithmetic wrapping used to be dangerous and how solidity changed. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Prefer safe arithmetic
keyIdea.text: Use Solidity 0.8+ for built-in overflow checks; audit or patch older code that relied on SafeMath semantics.

content.html:
Definition

Integer Overflow / Underflow

Understand arithmetic safety and historical mitigations.

What happens
  • Overflow: value exceeds max type and wraps to low values.
  • Underflow: subtracting more than current unsigned value wraps to a large number.
  • Effect: logic relying on numeric bounds can be broken, leading to asset misallocation.
Example: an 8-bit value at 255 plus 1 wrapped to 0 on older runtimes; modern Solidity reverts instead.
Mitigations
Use Solidity version 0.8 or later, which reverts on out-of-range arithmetic. When working with legacy code, apply SafeMath-like checks or rewrite logic to include explicit bounds verification.
Pro tip: enforce numeric sanity checks before writing state.
Common mistake: assuming libraries using older compilers inherit safe arithmetic automatically.
Key Takeaway

Prefer built-in arithmetic checks from modern compilers and validate or patch legacy contracts that rely on wrapping behavior.

screens.title: Front-running and transaction ordering
screens.subtitle: How mempool visibility enables ordering attacks

narration.text: Front-running is an economic attack that leverages the visibility of pending transactions in the mempool. An attacker watches for a profitable pending transaction, then submits their own transaction with a higher gas price so miners include it first. The attacker benefits from the state change—commonly seen in trading scenarios—before the original transaction executes. Because transaction order matters for many protocols, designing to minimize order dependence reduces risk. A common mitigation is a commit-reveal scheme where participants first submit a hashed commitment and reveal it in a later transaction; this prevents an observer from learning and frontrunning the action in the mempool. Another approach is to batch or pool sensitive state changes so they execute atomically at predictable times. A misconception is that simply increasing gas price protects honest users; gas does not prevent a determined adversary who can always outbid. Concrete scenario: a large buy order for a token can be frontrun by an automated bot that buys first and sells after the price moves. The question to keep in mind: can your protocol tolerate transaction-order manipulation or does it need a commit-reveal or batching approach?

keyIdea.title: Reduce order dependence
keyIdea.text: Design protocols so mempool visibility does not allow profitable manipulation; use commit-reveal or batching where needed.

content.html:
Core Concept

Front-running and Transaction Ordering

Understand how mempool visibility creates economic attack opportunities and mitigation patterns.

Why it matters
  • Pending transactions are visible; bots can react and submit priority transactions.
  • Order-sensitive logic like auctions and large trades is exposed to manipulation.
  • Mitigation changes protocol design rather than relying solely on gas economics.
Practical patterns
Commit-reveal schemes hide intent until after commitments are recorded. Batching or oracle-driven finalization reduces the window of opportunistic ordering. Where appropriate, use time-locked or aggregated settlement to reduce immediate ordering effects.
Example: commit a bid hash, reveal later to prevent frontrunning the bid.
Common mistake: assuming higher gas price deters attackers; it only raises cost.
Key Takeaway

If your protocol’s outcome depends on transaction order, adopt design patterns like commit-reveal or batching to limit economic exploits.

screens.title: OpenZeppelin Contracts and Access Control
screens.subtitle: Use community-vetted components to reduce risk

narration.text: OpenZeppelin Contracts are standardized, community-reviewed implementations of common smart contract components such as tokens, access control, and security utilities. Using these libraries reduces risk because they are audited by many teams and frequently updated to reflect best practices. Two commonly used patterns are Ownable for single-owner administration and AccessControl for role-based permissions. Ownable is simple and effective when one administrator is responsible for management tasks. AccessControl is more flexible, allowing multiple granular roles like PAUSER_ROLE and ADMIN_ROLE with specific allowed actions. Concrete example: inherit Ownable to protect administrative functions like emergencyStop, or inherit AccessControl and define a PAUSER_ROLE to allow multiple addresses to pause contract operations. A misconception is that libraries remove the need for design review; they reduce the chance of basic mistakes but you still must wire permissions correctly and limit privileges. When using OpenZeppelin, always review the specific contract versions you import and ensure your deployment and initialization grant roles intentionally. Final reflection: which administrative actions in your contracts should be single-owner versus multi-role? OpenZeppelin Contracts and Access Control means openzeppelin reduces risk but requires correct integration and minimal privileges for admin functions.. In practical terms, use community-vetted components to reduce risk. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Prefer vetted building blocks
keyIdea.text: OpenZeppelin reduces risk but requires correct integration and minimal privileges for admin functions.

content.html:
Architecture

OpenZeppelin & Access Control

Leverage audited contracts for ownership, role management, and security primitives.

Ownable
Provides a single owner address with onlyOwner modifier to protect functions. Ideal for simple projects where a single authority must act.
Example usage: protect emergency stop or treasury withdrawal with onlyOwner so only the deployer or a delegated admin can act.
AccessControl
Role-based permissions allow multiple, scoped administrators. Define roles for pausing, upgrading, or other sensitive operations and grant them to specific addresses.
Architectural choice: prefer AccessControl when multiple teams or signers must share duties safely.
Integration checklist
  • Import specific OpenZeppelin versions and review changelogs.
  • Grant roles intentionally; avoid default admin permissions for many accounts.
  • Combine role checks with pausable or multi-sig where needed for high-risk actions.

narration.text: Choosing between Ownable and AccessControl depends on governance needs. Ownable gives a single privileged address that can change critical state or execute administrative functions. It’s simple and easy to reason about, which reduces surface area for mistakes. AccessControl, by contrast, lets you define multiple roles with distinct capabilities. For example, you might grant a PAUSER_ROLE to a set of addresses able to pause the contract, while a separate ADMIN_ROLE can upgrade or change parameters. Concrete example: use Ownable for a small project where the deployer is the administrator, but use AccessControl for protocols with multiple teams or where operational duties should be partitioned. A misconception is that AccessControl is always safer; if roles are granted without careful limits, you can unintentionally expand privileges. Another practical point: AccessControl requires explicit role setup after deployment, so include initialization logic to assign the correct admin accounts. The closing question: which model maps more clearly to your project’s operational responsibilities and least privileges? Ownable vs AccessControl means use ownable for small-scope admin control; use accesscontrol when roles and multiple actors need separation of duties.. In practical terms, choosing single-owner or role-based permissions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Match permissions to governance
keyIdea.text: Use Ownable for small-scope admin control; use AccessControl when roles and multiple actors need separation of duties.

content.html:
Comparison

Ownable vs AccessControl

Weigh simplicity against flexibility and the risk of over-privileging accounts.

Ownable — Pros & Cons
  • Pros: simple, easy to audit, clear authority.
  • Cons: single point of failure unless combined with multisig.
Best for smaller teams or clear single-admin flows.
AccessControl — Pros & Cons
  • Pros: granular roles, separation of duties, flexible governance.
  • Cons: more complexity, must carefully assign and manage roles.
Best for protocols with multiple operators or staged responsibilities.
Key Takeaway

Choose the simplest model that enforces least privilege and integrates with your governance or multisig strategy.

screens.title: Auditing and Formal Verification
screens.subtitle: When to engage experts and when to apply proofs

narration.text: External auditing and formal verification are complementary risk-reduction activities. An audit is a human-driven review: security experts read the code, run tests, and perform tools-based analysis to find likely vulnerabilities and recommend fixes. Formal verification is a mathematical proof that a contract adheres to a specification. Audits are practical and broadly applicable; formal verification is expensive and usually reserved for the highest-value contracts or those that must meet strict correctness guarantees. Concrete example: a decentralized exchange handling billions needs an audit and may also formalize core settlement invariants for verification. A common misconception is that an audit guarantees absolute safety; audits reduce risk but cannot prove absence of bugs. Formal verification does provide stronger guarantees for specified properties but requires precise, often simplified specifications and significant effort. Practical process: minimize complexity, write clear specifications for the properties you need to verify, run audits, and consider formal proofs for settlement-critical components. Final reflection: which core invariants in your protocol would you require a proof for, and which can be validated through audits and monitoring? Auditing and Formal Verification means use audits broadly and reserve formal verification for critical invariants where mathematical guarantees are needed.. In practical terms, when to engage experts and when to apply proofs. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Layered assurance
keyIdea.text: Use audits broadly and reserve formal verification for critical invariants where mathematical guarantees are needed.

content.html:
Process Flow

Auditing & Formal Verification

Understand when to use human review and when to invest in proofs.

External Audit
Independent teams review code, tests, and architecture to identify vulnerabilities. Audits provide actionable recommendations and are practical for wide adoption.
Misconception: audits remove all risk. Reality: audits reduce risk but cannot cover every state-space path or future changes.
Formal Verification
Use mathematical proofs to show a contract satisfies a precise specification. Best for core invariants that must never fail, but more time-consuming and costly.
Practical step: write clear specifications for invariants you need to prove and simplify code paths where possible.
Key Takeaway

Combine audits for coverage and formal verification for critical invariants; both require simple, well-scoped code for best results.

screens.title: Secure Coding Checklist and Failsafes
screens.subtitle: Practical items to include before deployment

narration.text: Before deploying a contract that holds value, run a secure coding checklist to catch common mistakes. Start by ensuring inputs are validated with require and revert where appropriate. Prefer minimal, auditable code: split responsibilities across small contracts and avoid unnecessary complexity. For randomness, never rely on block attributes alone; use an oracle-based randomness source when outcomes must be unpredictable. Implement failsafes such as pausable controls or multi-signature wallets for administrative actions so that a single compromised key cannot cause catastrophic loss. Concrete example: add a pause function protected by onlyOwner or a PAUSER_ROLE and require consensus for emergency withdrawal via a multisig wallet. A typical misconception is that pausable features are a liability because they can be abused; in practice, they reduce blast radius if access is properly controlled and coupled with transparency. Final takeaway: adopt the checklist, map high-risk functions, and add monitoring and alerts to detect suspicious activity early. Which single fail-safe will you add first to your project? Secure Coding Checklist and Failsafes means validate inputs, minimize complexity, avoid insecure randomness, and add failsafes like pausable controls and multisig for admin actions.. In practical terms, practical items to include before deployment. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Checklist prevents surprises
keyIdea.text: Validate inputs, minimize complexity, avoid insecure randomness, and add failsafes like pausable controls and multisig for admin actions.

content.html:
Best Practices

Secure Coding Checklist & Failsafes

Concrete items to include in your deployment checklist.

Checklist items
  • Input validation with require and clear revert messages.
  • Apply checks-effects-interactions where external calls occur.
  • Use OpenZeppelin guards like nonReentrant and AccessControl.
  • Prefer Solidity 0.8+ for safe arithmetic and audit legacy code.
Failsafes & monitoring
Implement pausable controls, emergencyStop functions, and multi-signature wallets for high-risk operations. Add on-chain monitoring and alerts for unusual activity patterns.
Misconception: pausable contracts are inherently risky. In reality, properly controlled pause functionality limits damage during incidents.
Key Takeaway

A checklist and a small set of failsafes reduce exposure and make auditing and incident response far simpler.

narration.text: Let’s summarize the most important ideas to remember. Reentrancy is an attack where an external contract calls back into a function before it finished, enabling repeated withdrawals. The Checks-Effects-Interactions pattern prevents such attacks by validating conditions, updating state first, then making external calls. Integer overflow and underflow historically allowed values to wrap; modern Solidity versions revert on out-of-range arithmetic, but always check legacy code. These three ideas form the foundation of defensive smart contract design: prevent stale-state observation, enforce numeric safety, and prefer clear ordering for any external interaction. Use these short definitions as memory hooks while you review code: if you see external calls and state changes in the same function, ask whether state was updated first. If numbers are critical, confirm the compiler's arithmetic behavior or add explicit checks. These habits greatly reduce the most common catastrophic errors.

keyIdea.title: Short memory aids
keyIdea.text: Reentrancy, ordering, and numeric safety are the first checks when reviewing contract code.

content.html:
What to Remember

Key Concepts — Part 1

Compact definitions to keep at hand while coding and reviewing.

Reentrancy
An external call triggers a callback into the original contract before it finishes, enabling repeated actions like withdrawals.
Checks-Effects-Interactions
Validate inputs, update state, then perform external calls to avoid stale-state exploits.
Integer Overflow/Underflow
Arithmetic wrap-around that historically caused incorrect values; modern Solidity reverts on these errors.
Summary

When reviewing code, first look for external calls and numeric operations: confirm ordering and arithmetic safety before deployment.

narration.text: Finish with library and process reminders. OpenZeppelin Contracts provide audited implementations of common components such as tokens, ownership, and reentrancy guards; use them to avoid reinventing security-critical code. Ownable is a simple single-owner model; AccessControl provides role-based permissions when duties are split. Finally, auditing and formal verification are part of a trustworthy release strategy: audits give broad coverage and expert review, while formal verification provides mathematical guarantees for precisely specified properties. Use both where appropriate and reduce code complexity to make both processes tractable. As a practical rule: adopt OpenZeppelin for standard primitives, restrict administrative privileges with least-privilege principles, and plan audits for contracts that hold meaningful value. If a property must never fail—such as conservation of funds in a settlement contract—consider formal verification for that invariant. Key Concepts — Part 2 means prefer audited libraries, least-privilege access models, and a plan for audits or formal proofs when value is at stake.. In practical terms, libraries, access control, and verification. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Use community tools and verification
keyIdea.text: Prefer audited libraries, least-privilege access models, and a plan for audits or formal proofs when value is at stake.

content.html:
What to Remember

Key Concepts — Part 2

Practical library and process decisions that lower risk.

OpenZeppelin
A library of audited contract implementations and utilities that reduce the need for custom security code.
Ownable / AccessControl
Patterns for authorization: Ownable for single owner, AccessControl for multiple scoped roles.
Audit & Formal Verification
Audits catch likely issues; formal verification proves properties for carefully specified behavior where needed.
Final Takeaway

Combine vetted libraries, least-privilege access control, checks-effects-interactions, and an audit strategy to protect funds and reduce operational risk.
